name: Ecuador
card_headline: Ecuador's homicides are down about 8 percent in 2026 but remain near record levels, as Noboa renews emergency rule, deepens US military ties and denies a US base.
card_summary: Ecuador recorded 9,216 homicides in 2025 and 6,285 in the first nine months of 2026, about 23 a day. President Daniel Noboa recognised a new internal armed conflict in June, renewed a state of exception in eight provinces on 11 November, and works with US forces while denying a US base at Taura. Voters rejected foreign bases in November 2025. Prisons are still deadly, El Niño blackouts began in September, and local elections are on 29 November.
card_local: Primicias counts 190 multiple-victim killings in nine months of 2026, with August the worst month since 2014, and reports a 30-day renewal of emergency rule in eight provinces. [1][2]
card_international: Reuters reports more than 300,000 people displaced by violence, and Al Jazeera, relaying AFP, reports Noboa denying a US base at Taura while US aircraft and tents appear there. [3][4]
card_scholar: Crisis Group (November 2025) finds the military-led crackdown produced a brief drop in violence that did not last, and InSight Crime (October 2026) says the approach has not produced lasting results. [5][6]
context_md: Daniel Noboa of the National Democratic Action (ADN) took office in November 2023 to finish Guillermo Lasso's term and won a full four-year term in April 2025 with 55.6 percent in the runoff against Luisa Gonzalez. [7] On 9 January 2024 he declared an internal armed conflict and ordered the armed forces to neutralise 22 criminal groups. [8] Crisis Group describes a country that went from one of South America's safest to its most violent in under a decade, helped by the dollar, busy Pacific ports and weak border control. [5] Los Choneros and Los Lobos lead organised crime, and both are linked to Mexican cartels. [5] Voters approved nine security reforms in April 2024, then rejected four Noboa-backed proposals in November 2025, including one to allow foreign military bases. [7] The United States designated four Ecuadorian gangs as foreign terrorist organisations in August 2025. [7]

sections.title: The violence: 9,216 killed in 2025, an 8 percent fall in 2026 that leaves the second worst year
sections.body_md:
Ecuador recorded 9,216 homicides in 2025, a rate of 51 per 100,000 and about eight times the rate of a decade earlier. [3] That was up more than 30 percent from 7,063 in 2024. [9] El Universo puts 2025 at about 9,300 violent deaths, so counts vary slightly by source. [10] Primicias counts 6,285 victims from January to September 2026, 8.1 percent below the same months of 2025, or about 23 a day. [1] The government says homicides in March fell 28 percent from a year earlier. [9]

The fall hides a spike in massacres. Primicias logged 190 events with three or more deaths in nine months, killing 667 people, and August alone had 32 events and 117 victims, the most in one month since 2014. Guayas holds 43.2 percent of the events, and Guayas, Manabi, El Oro and Los Rios together hold 83.7 percent. [1]

The gangs keep splitting. Crisis Group counted at least 37 groups in 2024, of which the government designated 22 as terrorist organisations. [5] ACLED describes a turf war between Los Lobos and Los Choneros, and says Los Lobos is also fighting its Sao Box faction over illegal gold mining in El Oro. [11] InSight Crime says arrests of leaders have fuelled infighting rather than ending the groups. [6] Extortion complaints rose from 1,616 in 2019 to 23,080 in 2024 and fell to 16,131 in 2025, a decline InSight Crime says may reflect victims who no longer trust the police enough to report. [12]

More than 300,000 people have left their homes over three years, according to UNHCR and the Ombudsman's Office as reported by Reuters. Ecuador does not legally recognise displacement caused by violence, and officials told Reuters they did not know which agency handles it. [3] ACLED's December 2025 count is lower, about 132,000 internally displaced since 2021, so totals depend on the source. [11]

lenses.local: Primicias's tally shows a national decline alongside a record month of multiple-victim killings in August. [1]
lenses.international: Reuters and Al Jazeera carry the government's claims of falling homicides next to rights groups' doubts and the displacement count. [3][9]
lenses.scholar: ACLED and InSight Crime describe fragmenting gangs, and InSight Crime doubts that the extortion decline is real. [11][12]

sections.title: The legal frame: a new armed-conflict decree with pardons for security forces and immunity for foreign troops
sections.body_md:
Noboa declared an internal armed conflict on 9 January 2024. [8] On 18 June 2026 he signed Decree 424, which recognises a new internal armed conflict and revokes decrees 111 of January 2024, 218 of April 2024 and 55 of July 2025. In a video he called the groups "narcoterroristas". The decree names no specific groups. [13]

The decree says the state will receive international cooperation, that forces from allied countries will deploy in the most affected provinces, and that foreign personnel have immunity under applicable agreements. [13] The president will grant pardons or reduce sentences for military, police and civilians involved in operations, and the decree urges the National Assembly to grant amnesties. [14] Primicias links the decree to Noboa's recent meeting with US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon. [13]

Human Rights Watch's July 2026 report, A Dangerous Partnership, examines joint operations on 1 to 6 March in San Martin, on the Colombian border. Ecuador said the target was facilities of the Border Commands. HRW found no credible evidence that three properties burned or struck from the air were tied to criminal groups, and says four dairy workers were detained and tortured. It urges Ecuador to reassess its finding that an armed conflict exists. [15]

Colombian President Gustavo Petro said on 17 March that bombs fell near civilian farms, cited 27 charred bodies and called Ecuador's explanation not credible. Al Jazeera adds that The New York Times reported on 24 March that Ecuadorian soldiers burned and then bombed a dairy farm near the border. [9]

lenses.local: Vistazo's report on the decree quotes no critics or legal experts. [14]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera carries Petro's claim and the New York Times report on the border strikes. [9]
lenses.scholar: HRW asks Ecuador to reassess its armed-conflict finding, and InSight Crime says the militarised approach has not produced lasting results. [15][6]

sections.title: States of exception: renewed again on 11 November, with more than 2,000 detained
sections.body_md:
Decree 498 of 15 September 2026 declared a 60-day state of exception in eight mostly coastal provinces, ending 15 November. On 11 November Noboa signed Decree 532, renewing it for 30 days in El Oro, Esmeraldas, Guayas, Los Rios, Manabi, Pichincha, Santa Elena and Santo Domingo de los Tsachilas. [2]

The renewal keeps the terms of Decree 498: it suspends the inviolability of the home and of correspondence, allows temporary requisition of goods and services, and deploys the armed forces with the National Police. Decree 532 does not say whether a curfew applies. An earlier curfew ran from midnight to 5 a.m. on 17 to 30 September in Guayas, Manabi, Los Rios and El Oro, and a separate curfew in five provinces ended the day before the renewal. Primicias cites more than 2,000 people detained as of 8 November. [2]

The Constitutional Court polices the tool. Expreso reports that it annulled the state of exception in five of the seven provinces decreed after the diesel-subsidy protests, upheld it in Carchi and Imbabura but rejected the curfew there, and on 13 March 2026 declared constitutional a 30-day renewal for organised crime (Decree 311). [16] Officials told Al Jazeera in April that they would keep using curfews and other measures. [9]

lenses.local: Primicias reports the renewal, the suspended rights and the detention figure. [2]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera reports the March curfew in four provinces and the government's promise of more. [9]
lenses.scholar: Crisis Group says the Constitutional Court has challenged several of the government's measures. [5]

sections.title: Prisons: 78 homicides in nine months, then eight dead in two riots on 22 October
sections.body_md:
Simultaneous riots on 22 October at Cotopaxi No. 1 in Latacunga and Pichincha No. 1 (El Inca) in Quito killed eight inmates and injured ten. Two more inmates were found strangled in Loja on 23 October. Interior Ministry open data count 78 prison homicides from January to September 2026, and Primicias calls the period one of relative calm, with levels below the five previous years except 2024. The system held 39,692 inmates at the end of September, 38.44 percent over capacity. [17]

The 2025 toll was far higher. Reuters, citing official data, reports 1,220 inmate deaths in 2025, at least 206 of them killed in gang clashes and other violence, up from 46 in 2024. Deaths from illness, suicide and undetermined causes rose 256 percent, amid a tuberculosis outbreak the government links to overcrowding. [18] Primicias cites 199 prison homicides for 2025 and flags a headline giving 206, so the count differs by source. [17]

The military has run key prisons since January 2024. Relatives and rights groups allege abuse and lack of food, and the government and military did not respond to Reuters. The El Encuentro maximum-security prison holds gang leaders and former vice president Jorge Glas, bars visits by lawyers and relatives, and a facility for more than 15,000 inmates is planned for 2027. [18] Primicias reported in February that the promised 15,000-place prison did not appear in public procurement as of 12 February. [19]

The Global Initiative against Transnational Organized Crime counts 717 inmates killed in prisons from 2018 to 2024. Its analyst Renato Rivera Rhon writes that sources estimate guards, police, military personnel and directors capture 20 to 30 percent of the value of illicit transactions inside, and that phones cost up to $1,500 under military control. [20] InSight Crime reports extortion networks still operate from prisons, including some the military administers. [12]

lenses.local: Primicias provides the October riot details and the official homicide series. [17]
lenses.international: Reuters documents the 2025 death toll, the tuberculosis outbreak and the allegations against the military. [18]
lenses.scholar: GI-TOC describes prison governance as a form of criminal state capture. [20]

sections.title: US ties: a base Noboa denies, a referendum he lost, and abuses documented by HRW
sections.body_md:
On 16 November 2025 voters rejected all four of Noboa's proposals: allowing foreign military bases, cutting public funding for political parties, creating a constituent assembly and shrinking Congress. [21] On the bases question, 60.58 percent voted no with 98 percent of tally sheets counted. [22]

Cooperation has deepened regardless. The Congressional Research Service reports that the US designated Los Choneros, Los Lobos, Chone Killers and Los Tiguerones as terrorist organisations, that US military personnel have been present in Manta since December 2025, and that the FBI opened a permanent Quito office in March 2026. US security assistance was $15.9 million in FY2024 and $12.5 million in FY2025, with $30 million in INCLE aid and $10 million in FMF specified for FY2026. A July 2025 agreement lets the US send some third-country nationals to Ecuador, up to 300 adult asylum seekers a year, and 121 had arrived from January to July 2026. [7]

AFP reported in October an unusual US presence at Taura air base: aircraft, dozens of tents and about 20 US military flights from June to mid-October. The then air force commander, General Mauricio Salazar, wrote in September asking the armed forces to clarify the legality, and was later removed. On 15 November Noboa said US personnel are there for temporary activities, that it is "an Ecuadoran base", and declined a journalist's request to visit. [4]

HRW says survivors of drone attacks on two fishing boats in early 2026 reported that armed US nationals detained them and handed them to the Salvadoran Coast Guard. The US Defense Department and Coast Guard denied responsibility, and HRW concludes US authorities most likely had some involvement or knowledge. [15] Al Jazeera adds that HRW calls the partnership perilous. [4] WOLA's Adam Isacson and John Walsh argued in March 2024 that US support should back investigators, journalists and civil society rather than a Bukele-style approach. [23]

lenses.local: Primicias reported the referendum count on the bases question the night of the vote. [22]
lenses.international: AP, via NPR, and AFP, via Al Jazeera, carry the referendum defeat and the Taura deployment. [21][4]
lenses.scholar: CRS documents the scale of US assistance, and HRW documents the abuses it says followed joint operations. [7][15]

sections.title: Politics: a working majority, a Constitutional Court that blocks him, and local elections on 29 November
sections.body_md:
Noboa won the April 2025 runoff with 55.6 percent against Luisa Gonzalez of the Citizen Revolution, and ADN has built an informal Assembly majority with smaller parties. [7] Expreso reports that the bloc relies on independents, a faction of Pachakutik and defectors from the opposition, and that the Assembly passed urgent laws and more than 70 resolutions in its first year. [16]

The Constitutional Court is the main check. Expreso counts 17 articles of the National Solidarity, Intelligence and Public Integrity laws temporarily suspended and two of five proposed partial constitutional reforms rejected. After the suspensions Noboa proposed a referendum to allow impeachment of constitutional judges. [16] On 16 October the Court ruled that the Reciprocal Trade Agreement with the US needs Assembly approval, calling this the first stage of its review. [24]

Subnational elections on 29 November were moved up from February 2027, with the electoral council citing El Nino. [25] Primicias reports that the electoral court suspended the Citizen Revolution for nine months and barred Luisa Gonzalez from running for the Manabi prefecture for Pachakutik. Guayaquil mayor Aquiles Alvarez was in pretrial detention from 10 February to 3 August and could not register for re-election. Ronald Farfan, a mayoral candidate in Huaquillas, and council candidate Cristian Rugel were killed in an armed attack. [25] ACLED warned in December of rising violence against political figures before the local elections. [11]

lenses.local: Expreso and Primicias supply the detail on the Assembly, the Court and the campaign. [16][25]
lenses.international: CRS describes ADN's informal majority and the scheduled 29 November vote. [7]
lenses.scholar: Mayorga and Thaler argue in the Journal of Democracy that Noboa's measures weakened judicial independence and constrained protest, and that the failed 2025 referendum showed the limits of his mandate. [26]

sections.title: Rights and information: critics called anti-patriots, a court order against a press group, and 71 percent of checked items distorted
sections.body_md:
Amnesty International reports that three years after the August 2023 Yasuni referendum the government has not fully implemented the result: the one-year deadline for oil withdrawal expired in August 2024, extraction continues, and the plan submitted to the Constitutional Court would extend the shutdown to 2034. It says a court fined two members of the YASunidos collective about $18,000 in total over campaign donation reporting, a discrepancy they put at 39 cents. It also cites a 2025 Organic Law on Social Transparency, bank account blocks for some civil society groups and Noboa's use of the term anti-patriots for critics. [27]

CPJ, the Inter-American Press Association and Voces del Sur condemned an April 2026 court order requiring the press freedom group Fundamedios to remove a publication that mentions a businessman, calling it a "deeply dangerous precedent". [28] BBC Mundo reports that Ecuador fell 31 places to 125th in Reporters Without Borders' 2026 ranking, from 68th in 2022, and cites HRW on extrajudicial executions, forced disappearances and arbitrary detentions by security forces. [8]

Ecuador Chequea logged 434 checks from January to June 2026 and rated 70.7 percent false, misleading or imprecise. It counted 66 AI-generated items, 54 of them false, and says fake posts impersonate outlets such as Primicias, El Universo and Diario Extra. A separate review of 131 presidential statements from May 2025 to May 2026 found about one in four completely true. [29] After Noboa's 24 May address, Lupa Media (29 checks) and Ecuador Chequea (42 checks) each rated about 30 percent of the claims as true. [30]

lenses.local: Ecuador Chequea and El Mercurio report on disinformation and on the accuracy of the president's claims. [29][30]
lenses.international: BBC Mundo reports the press freedom ranking fall and HRW's findings on security-force abuses. [8]
lenses.scholar: Amnesty and CPJ document the narrowing of civic space and press freedom. [27][28]

sections.title: Economy and power: slower growth, a US tariff fight and blackouts under a historic El Nino
sections.body_md:
The IMF's April outlook projects 2.5 percent growth in 2026, down from 3.7 percent in 2025, against a Noboa projection above 3 percent. The World Bank's April forecast is also 2.5 percent. [31] The IMF's $5 billion extended arrangement, approved in May 2024 and augmented in July 2025, completed its fourth review in December 2025, projecting gross reserves of $13.2 billion and public debt of 51.4 percent of GDP for 2026. [32] CRS says about $3.7 billion has been disbursed. [7] In his May address Noboa said poverty fell from 26 percent to 21.4 percent in 2025. [33]

The US is Ecuador's largest goods trading partner, at $17.6 billion in 2025. [7] A nonbinding trade agreement signed in March was meant to remove a 10 percent surcharge on about 53 percent of non-oil exports. That surcharge expired in July, and exporters' federation Fedexpor says a new 10 percent surcharge tied to a forced-labour investigation covers about 46 percent, with shrimp the most affected product. [24] CRS adds that the US imposed Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies in July, with Ecuador at 10 percent against 12.5 percent for most. [7]

Ecuador declared a red alert on 29 August for an El Nino projected at historic magnitude, with the heaviest effects from the last quarter of 2026 into early 2027. Primicias says hydropower drought is expected from September to March, and Coca Codo Sinclair, at 1,500 MW, supplies about 30 percent of hydro generation. [34] On 13 and 14 September blackouts of minutes to two hours hit Quito and parts of Guayas after sediment forced Coca Codo to cut its intake and the grid operator Cenace ordered emergency disconnections. Ecuador stopped buying Colombian power as prices rose from 33 cents per kWh on 5 August to an average of 88 cents from 7 September. [35]

lenses.local: Expreso and El Mercurio report the growth forecasts, the September blackouts and Colombian power prices. [31][35]
lenses.international: AP reports Noboa's poverty claim in his May address to the Assembly. [33]
lenses.scholar: The IMF's December review and CRS give the programme size, disbursements and trade figures. [32][7]

reporters.name: Alexander Garcia
reporters.bio: Bylines the Primicias count of 190 multiple-victim killings in nine months of 2026 and the September report on the El Nino red alert and power supply.
reporters.why: His data pieces supply many of the official-statistics tallies used in this draft.
reporters.label: Primicias, 23 October 2026

reporters.name: Gladys Rivadeneira
reporters.bio: Bylines the Primicias report on Decree 532, which renewed the state of exception in eight provinces on 11 November 2026.
reporters.why: Her report gives the decree's provinces, suspended rights and the earlier curfew dates.
reporters.label: Primicias, 11 November 2026

reporters.name: Valeria Alvear
reporters.bio: Bylines the Expreso review of the Noboa government's relations with the Assembly, the Constitutional Court and the United States, dated 23 May 2026.
reporters.why: The piece collects the Court's rulings against the government in one place.
reporters.label: Expreso, 23 May 2026

reporters.name: Andrea Salazar
reporters.bio: Bylines El Mercurio's report on the 13 and 14 September blackouts and its 26 May fact-check roundup of Noboa's address.
reporters.why: She covers both the power system and the accuracy of official claims.
reporters.label: El Mercurio, 15 September 2026

reporters.name: Yalile Loaiza
reporters.bio: Credited as general editor of Ecuador Chequea's January to June 2026 report on disinformation.
reporters.why: Her team's semester report is the best quantified view of false content in Ecuador this year.
reporters.label: Ecuador Chequea

reporters.name: Alexandra Valencia
reporters.bio: Co-bylines Reuters reports from Quito and Guayaquil on prison deaths (February 2026) and on displacement caused by gang violence (September 2026).
reporters.why: Reuters is the main wire source in this draft for prisons and displacement.
reporters.label: Reuters via The Star, 16 February 2026

reporters.name: Yury Garcia
reporters.bio: Co-bylines the same two Reuters reports on Ecuador's prison deaths and displacement.
reporters.why: His reporting from Guayaquil puts figures on families who left their neighbourhoods.
reporters.label: Reuters via Internazionale, 8 September 2026

reporters.name: Sean Doherty
reporters.bio: Author of the 15 October 2026 InSight Crime analysis of why Ecuador is losing its fight against organised crime.
reporters.why: His piece traces arrests of gang leaders and the July 2026 security plan.
reporters.label: InSight Crime

reporters.name: Renato Rivera Rhon
reporters.role: Senior analyst, Andean region, Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime
reporters.bio: Author of the January 2026 GI-TOC report Carceral Capture on criminal governance in Ecuador's prisons.
reporters.why: The report is the most detailed public account of how prisons are run by criminal groups.
reporters.label: GI-TOC

reporters.name: Tiziano Breda
reporters.bio: Author of ACLED's December 2025 Conflict Watchlist entry on Ecuador, covering 1 January to 28 November 2025.
reporters.why: He sets out the turf war between Los Lobos and Los Choneros and the risks for 2026.
reporters.label: ACLED

reporters.name: Adam Isacson
reporters.bio: Co-author with John Walsh of WOLA's March 2024 analysis of why Ecuador should not copy El Salvador's model.
reporters.why: The piece is older than most items here but is the clearest structural comparison with Bukele's approach.
reporters.label: WOLA

reporters.name: Kai M. Thaler
reporters.role: Assistant professor of global studies, University of California, Santa Barbara
reporters.bio: Co-author with Galo Mayorga of Crime, Crackdowns, and Democracy in Ecuador, Journal of Democracy, January 2026.
reporters.why: The article argues that Noboa's militarised response has weakened judicial independence without reducing violence.
reporters.label: Journal of Democracy

books.title: Assessing the Left Turn in Ecuador
books.author: Francisco Sanchez and Simon Pachano (eds.)
books.why: An edited volume on Correa's ten-year government, covering institutional change, corruption, social movements and the commodities boom. It explains the state that Noboa inherited.
books.label: Springer (Palgrave Macmillan)

books.title: Undoing Multiculturalism: Resource Extraction and Indigenous Rights in Ecuador
books.author: Carmen Martinez Novo
books.why: Two decades of fieldwork on why the Correa government did not deliver on Indigenous rights and how extraction was resisted, background for the Yasuni and mining disputes.
books.label: University of Pittsburgh Press

books.title: The CIA in Ecuador
books.author: Marc Becker
books.why: Uses released US surveillance files to study Ecuador's Cold War left, and relevant to readers asking about the long history of US security involvement.
books.label: Duke University Press

podcasts.title: Ecuador Says Extortion Is Down. The Reality Is More Complicated.
podcasts.why: An audio version of the Voss and Dudley analysis of whether the government's extortion figures hold up. The listing page gives no named host.

media.title: Drug War in Ecuador
media.creator: Marcel Mettelsiefen (PBS FRONTLINE)
media.where: Free on pbs.org/frontline, the PBS app and FRONTLINE on YouTube; premiered 11 November 2025.
media.why: Follows a priest, a governor and a grieving father to show how state violence, gang recruitment and inequality are tied together.

media.title: Ecuador: A Country at War with the Narcos
media.creator: Geraud Burin des Roziers (Ligne de Front)
media.where: Distributor listing page; broadcaster not stated.
media.why: Follows police and army operations in Guayaquil and profiles a mayor and a magistrate working against organised crime. It predates the 2025 and 2026 escalation.

factchecks.claim: The United States does not operate a military base in Ecuador; it is an Ecuadoran base.
factchecks.evidence: AFP reported unusual US aircraft, tents and infrastructure work at Taura air base, about 20 US military flights from June to mid-October, and documents referring to US soldiers. The scope of the US presence has not been disclosed, and the Pentagon, Southern Command and Ecuador's air force did not answer AFP. CRS separately reports US military personnel in Manta since December 2025. Ecuador's constitution bans foreign bases, and voters rejected lifting the ban in November 2025.

InSight Crime reports experts and officials say victims often do not report because they distrust police, and that smaller groups and opportunists now extort businesses, so the true number is likely higher.

sources.title: Ecuador says extortion is down; the reality is more complicated

scores.coverage_basis: Reuters, AP and AFP file on Ecuador regularly, mostly when a decree, prison riot or US deployment lands. [18][33][4] Local press output is dense (Primicias, Expreso, El Mercurio) and Crisis Group, InSight Crime, GI-TOC and ACLED publish steadily. [1][5][20]

severity.basis: Ecuador recorded 9,216 homicides in 2025 and 6,285 in the first nine months of 2026, with massacres at a monthly high in August. [3][1]
More than 300,000 people have been displaced by violence, 1,220 inmates died in 2025, and an El Nino red alert was declared. [3][18][34]
A rolling state of exception, alleged abuses in joint operations, a court order against a press group and a fall to 125th in press freedom. [2][15][28][8]
Growth is forecast at 2.5 percent under an IMF programme with public debt near 51 percent of GDP, and US tariffs hit about 46 percent of non-oil exports. [31][32][24]
Homicides are down about 8 percent but the 2026 level is still extreme, while militarisation, US presence and emergency rule have deepened. [1][6][4]

parts.basis: The US designated four Ecuadorian gangs as terrorist organisations, has personnel in Manta and Taura reports, and is Ecuador's largest goods trading partner. [7][4]
The US trade is worth $17.6 billion a year and Ecuador is a cocaine export hub whose ports shape trafficking routes. [7][5]
Crisis Group links Ecuadorian groups to Mexican cartels and ACLED notes Colombian armed groups are expanding on the border. [5][11]
Over 122,000 Ecuadorians sought asylum abroad in 2025, 93 percent of them in the US, and ACLED counts over 400,000 who left since 2021. [7][11]
A decree promising immunity to foreign troops and pardons for security forces, plus US operations on Ecuadorian soil, set a model other governments may copy. [13][15]

summary: Ecuador matters beyond its borders as a cocaine export hub, a test case for US-backed military crackdowns and a source of migrants, more than through trade or great-power rivalry. [5][7][15]
gi.up: A confirmed permanent US base, a collapse of order in Guayaquil's port, or a sharp rise in migration to the US.
gi.down: A sustained fall in homicides under civilian-led policing and an end to the open-ended emergency decrees.

gaps: Plan V and GK (Ecuador's investigative outlets) returned no usable pages in search, so their reporting is not cited; local sourcing leans on Primicias, Expreso, El Mercurio, Vistazo and Ecuador Chequea.

Mongabay Latam's 2026 Ecuador pieces (illegal mining, deforestation, Yasuni) were found in search but the site could not be fetched, so environment and mining are covered only through Amnesty, ACLED and Reuters.
State-run Ecuador TV, El Telegrafo and government agency sites were not consulted or cited; official figures come through Primicias, Reuters and the media that relay them.
WOLA's only Ecuador analysis located is from March 2024, so WOLA's current view is a gap.
The AFP investigation of Taura air base was read through Al Jazeera's summary; the US and Ecuadorian governments have not published the size or legal basis of the US presence.
Homicide, prison-death and displacement counts differ by source (9,216 vs about 9,300 for 2025; 199 vs 206 prison homicides; 300,000 vs 132,000 displaced) and are not reconciled here.
Claims by Colombian President Petro (27 charred bodies) and a New York Times report on a bombed dairy farm are relayed by Al Jazeera and were not independently checked.
The HRW report was read through its news release, the Crisis Group report through its first 100,000 characters, the Journal of Democracy essay through its abstract, and El Universo behind a paywall.
The RSF ranking (125th) and the Noboa poverty figures (21.4 percent) are relayed by BBC Mundo and AP and were not checked at source.
Local elections are on 29 November 2026, after the data date, so results are not covered.

local_md:
Primicias's tally shows a national decline alongside a record month of multiple-victim killings in August. [1]

Vistazo's report on the decree quotes no critics or legal experts. [14]

Primicias reports the renewal, the suspended rights and the detention figure. [2]

Primicias provides the October riot details and the official homicide series. [17]

Primicias reported the referendum count on the bases question the night of the vote. [22]

Expreso and Primicias supply the detail on the Assembly, the Court and the campaign. [16][25]

Ecuador Chequea and El Mercurio report on disinformation and on the accuracy of the president's claims. [29][30]

Expreso and El Mercurio report the growth forecasts, the September blackouts and Colombian power prices. [31][35]
international_md:
Reuters and Al Jazeera carry the government's claims of falling homicides next to rights groups' doubts and the displacement count. [3][9]

Al Jazeera carries Petro's claim and the New York Times report on the border strikes. [9]

Al Jazeera reports the March curfew in four provinces and the government's promise of more. [9]

Reuters documents the 2025 death toll, the tuberculosis outbreak and the allegations against the military. [18]

AP, via NPR, and AFP, via Al Jazeera, carry the referendum defeat and the Taura deployment. [21][4]

CRS describes ADN's informal majority and the scheduled 29 November vote. [7]

BBC Mundo reports the press freedom ranking fall and HRW's findings on security-force abuses. [8]

AP reports Noboa's poverty claim in his May address to the Assembly. [33]
scholar_md:
ACLED and InSight Crime describe fragmenting gangs, and InSight Crime doubts that the extortion decline is real. [11][12]

HRW asks Ecuador to reassess its armed-conflict finding, and InSight Crime says the militarised approach has not produced lasting results. [15][6]

Crisis Group says the Constitutional Court has challenged several of the government's measures. [5]

GI-TOC describes prison governance as a form of criminal state capture. [20]

CRS documents the scale of US assistance, and HRW documents the abuses it says followed joint operations. [7][15]

Mayorga and Thaler argue in the Journal of Democracy that Noboa's measures weakened judicial independence and constrained protest, and that the failed 2025 referendum showed the limits of his mandate. [26]

Amnesty and CPJ document the narrowing of civic space and press freedom. [27][28]

The IMF's December review and CRS give the programme size, disbursements and trade figures. [32][7]
